system_prompt: You are a careful and skilled AI assistant. Provide your best answer to the following prompt. Keep your response under 500 words.
response:
## The trolley problem as a genuine dilemma

The strongest version is not "five lives versus one - obvious utilitarianism." The strongest version is this:

The runaway trolley will kill five workers tied to the main line. You stand by a switch that diverts it to a side track, where it will kill *one* worker. The single worker is not culpable, is not consenting, would not be killed but for your action, and has - in your reasonable judgment - exactly as much moral standing and as many years of life remaining as each of the five.

This is a genuine dilemma because two of our deepest moral commitments collide and cannot both be satisfied:

- **Beneficence / outcomes.** Failing to save five when you could is a real and grave wrong.
- **The inviolability of persons.** Bringing about a person's death as a chosen consequence of your action - even as a side-effect of a redirect - treats them as a resource for others, in violation of the Kantian or rights-based intuition that persons are ends in themselves.

The dilemma sharpens in the *Footbridge* variant (Thomson 1985): the only way to stop the trolley is to push a large bystander off a bridge into its path. Most people who pull the switch in the original refuse to push the bystander, though the arithmetic is identical. That asymmetry - some actions permissible, others not, at the same five-vs-one cost - is the puzzle, and signals that our moral structure is richer than pure consequentialism captures.

## The strongest objection to a simple "save the five" calculation

The objection is *not* that one life equals five (the math is clear). It is that aggregating across persons treats them as interchangeable, denying what Nozick (1974) called the *separateness of persons*: there is no overarching being who experiences "the five deaths minus one" and prefers the latter. There are six distinct subjects, and one - the side-track worker - has done nothing to forfeit their life.

If lives may be traded by simple count, conclusions follow that nearly everyone rejects:

- A surgeon should kill one healthy patient to harvest organs for five dying ones (the *transplant case*).
- The state should conscript involuntary medical-research subjects whenever five future patients would benefit.
- Each of us is permanently obligated to give all spare resources wherever they save the most lives.

These are reductios. The simple calculation produces them; we resist them. So we are committed to some deontological side-constraint blocking aggregation - but we cannot formulate it precisely. The doctrine of double effect almost works; agent-relative permissions almost work; each has counterexamples.

That sustained tension - we cannot reduce the problem to pure consequentialism or pure deontology without losing moral truths - is what makes the trolley problem a *genuine* dilemma. It is one of the clearest tests we have that our moral intuitions are richer than any single ethical theory we have yet formulated.
